parts.problem_md:
Two charged metal spheres A and B are situated in a vacuum, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1.

![q4b-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics](assets/001-q4b-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 4.1**

The shortest distance between the surfaces of the spheres is 6.0 cm.

A movable point P lies along the line joining the centres of the two spheres, a distance *x* from the surface of sphere A.

The variation with distance *x* of the electric field E at point P is shown in Fig. 4.2.

![q4b-2-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics](assets/002-q4b-2-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 4.2**

(i) Use Fig. 4.2 to explain whether the two spheres have charges of the same, or opposite, sign.

[2]

(ii) A proton is at point P where *x* = 5.0 cm.

Use data from Fig. 4.2 to determine the magnitude of the acceleration of the proton.

acceleration = ................................. m s<sup>–2</sup> [3]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Use Fig. 4.2 to explain whether the two spheres have charges of the same, or opposite, sign:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one ****from:**

- According to the graph the electric field E close to sphere A is positive and close to sphere B is negative; **[1 mark]**
- The electric fields are in opposite directions; **[1 mark]**
- There is a point on the graph between the spheres where the field strength is zero; **[1 mark]** **AND**
- So the charges on the spheres have the same sign; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Use data from Fig. 4.2 to determine the magnitude of the acceleration of the proton:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from sphere x = 5.0 cm

From the data booklet:

- Elementary charge, $e$ = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
- Rest mass of a proton, $m_{p}$ = 1.67 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg

Draw lines on the graph to determine the electric field E at x:

![file-000-45](assets/003-file-000-45.png)

- The electric field is −3.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> V m<sup>−1</sup>
- The magnitude of the electric field is therefore, 3.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> V m<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Consider the equations needed to calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the proton:

- Newton's second law: $F=ma$
- Electric force: $F=EQ$

Combine the two equations and rearrange to make acceleration $a$ the subject:

- $EQ=ma$
- $a=\frac{EQ}{m}$** [1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation to calculate acceleration $a$:

- $a = \frac{( 3 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 1.6 \times 10^{- 19} )}{1.67 \times 10^{- 27} }$
- $a = 2.87 \times 10^{11 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-2} } = 2.9 \times 10^{11 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{-2} } ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Part (i) is a tricky question:*

  - *The **equilibrium position** is in the **middle** where the **fields cancel out** - that couldn’t happen if they had opposite charges, the field would be in the same direction for all values of x*
  - *Q** represents the **charge of the particle** in the** field**, not the charge of the spheres*
- *In part (ii) think about all the **equations** you know for **force** and combine them*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Calculate the kinetic energy of an α particle travelling at a speed of 3.50 × 10^7 m s^–1. Ek = 4.09 × 10^–12 J

Calculate the closest distance of approach for a head-on collision between an  $α$ particle travelling at a speed of 3.50 × 10<sup>7</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>and a gold nucleus for which the proton number is 79.

Assume that the gold nucleus remains stationary during the collision.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Kinetic energy of particle, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = 4.09 × 10<sup>–12</sup> J (from part a)

From data page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>
- Charge of an electron, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19 </sup>C

Calculate charge of alpha particle and gold nucleus:

- An alpha particle is a helium nucleus with 2 protons and 2 neutrons
- Charge of alpha particle, $Q_{α}$= +2*e* **AND** Charge of gold nucleus, $Q_{gold}$ = +79*e ***[1 mark]**

Calculate the closest distance of approach:

- The kinetic energy lost by the alpha particle = gain in electric potential energy as it approaches the gold nucleus
- Gain in potential energy, *E*<sub>*P*</sub>  =$\frac{Q_{α}Q_{gold}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ = loss in *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* ***[1 mark]**
- *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *=$\frac{Q_{α}Q_{gold}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ therefore, *r *=$\frac{Q_{α}Q_{gold}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}E_{k}}$
- *r* =$\frac{2 \times 79 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} )^{2}}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 8.85 \times 10^{- 12} ) \times ( 4.09 \times 10^{- 12} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- *r* = 8.89 × 10<sup>–15</sup> m = 8.89 fm **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The equation for electric potential energy is given at the start of your paper on the formula page. This is the energy involved in bringing a charge **q ** from infinity to a distance **r**  from a point charge **Q.*

parts.problem_md:
The potential on the surface of a charged sphere is +220 kV. The sphere has a radius of 12 cm.

Calculate the charge stored on the surface of the sphere.

The charge may be assumed to act as a point charge situated at the centre of the sphere.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the charge stored on the surface of the sphere:

List the known quantities:

- Radius of the sphere, *r* = 12 cm = 0.12 m
- Electric potential, *V* = +220 kV = +220 × 10<sup>3</sup> V
- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$= 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup> (from the data page)

Use the equation for electric potential:

- Electric potential,  $V=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r}$
- Rearrange:  $Q=4πε_{0}rV$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the charge stored on the surface of the sphere, *Q*:

- Substitute:  $Q$ = 4π × (8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup>) × 0.12 × (220 × 10<sup>3</sup>) **[1 mark]**
- Charge stored: * *$Q$* *= 2.9 × 10<sup>–6</sup> C (2.9 µC) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *When carrying out calculations involving charged spheres, we are usually told that we can assume the charge acts as a point charge at the centre of the sphere. This means we may treat the charge **and **the electric potential on the surface to be the same as that of a point charge at the centre of the sphere.*

V = 86 900 = 87 000 V (87 kV)

A proton is moved from infinity to a point in the electric field produced by the charge.

(i) State the potential difference between infinity and the point 30 cm away from the charge

[1]

(ii) Calculate the work done on the proton to move it from infinity to the point 30 cm away from the charge.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Electric potential 30 cm from the charge = 87 kV (from part c)
- Elementary charge, $e$ = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C (from data page)

(i) State the potential difference between infinity and 30 cm away from the charge:

- The potential is defined as 0 V at infinity
- Hence, potential difference:  Δ*V* = 87 – 0 = 87 kV **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the work done moving the charge:

- Work done:  $\DeltaW=Q\DeltaV$
- $\DeltaW$ = (1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) × (87 000) **[1 mark]**
- $\DeltaW$ = 1.4 × 10<sup>–14</sup> J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember the definition of potential at a point is the work done per unit of charge in moving a (test) charge from infinity (where potential is 0 V) to that point. *

> *You should be comfortable assigning a value of 0 V to a point infinitely far away, so you can work out the potential difference between infinity and a point in a field very easily, using the equation *$V=\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$* to calculate the value of the potential itself any distance **r** from the charge **Q**.*

parts.problem_md:
Two charges are separated by a distance of 23 cm, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![18-2-3c-m-point-charge-and-elec-field-sq-cie-a-level](assets/005-18-2-3c-m-point-charge-and-elec-field-sq-cie-a-l.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the distance, in mm, from the −22.1 μC to the point between the two charges, where the resultant electric potential is zero.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the distance, in mm, from the −22.1 μC to the point between the two charges, where the resultant electric potential is zero:

List the known quantities:

- Separation, *r *= 23 cm = 0.23 m
- Charge 1, *Q*<sub>*1*</sub> = −22.1 μC =  −22.1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C
- Charge 2, *Q*<sub>*2*</sub> = +5.4 μC = 5.4 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C
- $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>−1</sup>

Draw a diagram of the situation:

![ddc09216-64df-473f-aa57-7fcb4f7bdc63](assets/006-ddc09216-64df-473f-aa57-7fcb4f7bdc63.jpeg)

Use the equation for the electric potential to obtain an expression for the electric potential when it is zero:

- $V=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r}$
- Potential due to −22.1 μC charge is: $\frac{( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) x}$
- Potential due to +5.4 μC charge is: $\frac{( + 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) ( 0.23 - x )}$
- So, $\frac{( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) x} + \frac{( + 5.4 \times 10^{-6} } )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) ( 0.23 - x )} = 0$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to obtain a value for *x*:

- $\frac{( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} )}{ x} = \frac{( - 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} )}{ ( 0.23 - x )}$
- $( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} ) ( 0.23 - x ) = ( - 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} ) x$
- $( - 5.083 \times 10^{- 6} ) + ( 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} ) x = ( - 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} ) x$
- $( - 5.083 \times 10^{- 6} ) = ( - 2.75 \times 10^{- 5} ) x$ **[1 mark]**
- So, $x = \frac{( - 5.083 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( - 2.75 \times 10^{- 5} )} = 0.184 \mathrm{m} = 184 \text{mm}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Electric potential is a scalar quantity, so the sum of the **resultant electric potential = 0**. In the method shown above the quantities from the question are substituted into the equation for electric potential. You could **rearrange and substitute at the end** too, sometimes it is easier to see a rearrangement with **numbers**. *

parts.problem_md: State the relation between electric field and potential.
parts.solution_md:
The relation between electric field and potential is:

- Field strength = negative electric potential gradient  **OR ** $E=-\frac{\DeltaV}{\Deltar}$; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark] **

Fig. 1.1 shows the electric field lines around a particle with charge q. State and explain whether the particle is positively or negatively charged. [Mark scheme: The particle is positively charged; the field lines are directed away from the particle]

parts.solution_md:

- Potential gradient acts in the opposite direction to the field; **[1 mark]**

- Electric potential and distance are inversely proportional **OR** $V\propto\frac{1}{r}$; **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows the electric field lines around a particle with charge q.

A stationary proton is placed at point A, which is a distance of 0.1 nm from the particle. The proton is released and moves to point B, which is a distance of 0.5 nm from the particle.

The potential difference between A and B is 23 V.

Show that the particle has the same charge as two protons.
parts.solution_md:
Show that the particle has the same charge as two protons:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from the particle to A, $r_{1}$ = 0.1 nm = 0.1 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
- Distance from the particle to B, $r_{2}$ = 0.5 nm = 0.5 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
- Potential difference between A and B, $\DeltaV$ = 23 V
- Coulumb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>−1</sup>
- Elementary charge, $e$ = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C (from the data page)

Use the equation for change in electric potential:

- Electric potential:  $V=\frac{q}{4πε_{0}r}$ (from the data page)
- Change in electric potential:  $\Delta V = \frac{q}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \epsilon_{0} } ( \frac{1}{r} _{1} - \frac{1}{r} _{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation and substitute the values to calculate the charge:

- $q = \frac{4 \mathrm{\pi } \epsilon_{0} \Delta V}{( \frac{1}{r} _{1} - \frac{1}{r} _{2} )}$
- $q = \frac{23}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) ( \frac{1}{0.1 \times 10^{-9} } } - \frac{1}{0.5 \times 10^{- 9} } )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $q=3.2\times10^{-19}C$ **AND**
- The charge of a proton is $e=1.6\times10^{-19}C$, so $q=2e$; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The charge *$q$* in the equation refers to the charge producing the field, which in this case is the particle.*

parts.problem_md:
Three charges are fixed at the corners of a right-angled triangle as shown in Fig. 1.1. The length of the horizontal and vertical sides are both *d. *

![7-5-s-q--q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](assets/012-7-5-s-q-q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Show that the electric potential at point P, halfway between the −2Q and −6Q charge is:

$V_{p}=-\frac{2Q}{\sqrt{2}d\mathrm{πε}_{0}}$
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Charge on Q<sub>1</sub> = −2Q
- Charge on Q<sub>2 </sub>= +4Q
- Charge on Q<sub>3</sub> = −6Q
- Distance from Q<sub>1</sub> to Q<sub>2</sub> = *d*
- Distance from Q<sub>2</sub> to Q<sub>3</sub> = *d*

From the data sheet:

- Electric potential, *V* =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$

Calculate the distance from each charge to point P, *h*:

- (2*h*)<sup>2</sup> = *d*<sup>2</sup> + *d*<sup>2</sup> **OR** *h*<sup>2</sup> = $( \frac{d}{2} )^{2} + ( \frac{d}{2} )^{2}$
- *h*<sup>2</sup> =$\frac{2d^{2}}{4}$
- *h* =$\frac{\sqrt{2}d}{2}$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total electric potential at the point P, $V_{p}$ :

- $V_{p}$= $V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3}$
- $V_{p}$ =  $( - \frac{2 Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} ( \text{bevelled} \frac{ \sqrt{2} d}{2} )} ) + ( \frac{4 Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} ( \text{bevelled} \frac{ \sqrt{2} d}{2} )} ) + ( - \frac{6 Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} ( \text{bevelled} \frac{ \sqrt{2} d}{2} )} )$  **[1 mark]**
- $V_{p}$ =  $( - \frac{2 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } ) + ( \frac{4 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } ) + ( - \frac{6 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } )$
- $V_{p}$= $( - \frac{4 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } )$ =$( - \frac{2 Q}{ \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } )$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Make sure to label the diagram if this makes it easier to calculate the correct lengths. The key is to realise that P is equidistant from all the charges. Remember that electric potential is scalar so the direction doesn’t matter!*

parts.problem_md:
Before the discovery of quarks, scientists speculated that the subatomic particles might be made up of smaller particles.

If an electron was made up of three smaller, identical particles with charge *q *which are brought in from an infinite distance to the vertices of an equilateral triangle, it would have the arrangement shown in Fig. 1.2.

![7-5-s-q--q3b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](assets/014-7-5-s-q-q3b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Show that the work done in forming an electron consisting of three identical particles, as shown in Fig. 1.2, is:

$ΔW=\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{e^{2}}{3r}$

Where:

- The distance *r* is the radius of an electron which is 2.82 fm
- *e* is the charge of an electron
- $ε_{0}$ is the permittivity of free space
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Length of side of equilateral triangle, *r* = 2.82 fm = 2.82 × 10<sup>-15</sup> m

From data sheet:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>-12</sup> F m<sup>-1</sup>
- Magnitude of the charge of an electron, *e* = 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C

Determine size of charge of each particle, *q*:

- *q *= $\frac{1}{3}$*e ***[1 mark]**

Work done bringing second electron into the triangle, $\DeltaW_{2}$ :

- Work done, ∆*W* = *q*∆*V*
- Electric potential, *V* = $\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$
- ∆*V =*$V_{2}-V_{\infty}$* *– where $V_{2}$ is the electric potential at the second vertex due to the existing electron
- $\DeltaW_{2}$= $1 \frac{1}{3} e \times ( \frac{1 \frac{1}{3} e}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} r} - 0 )$
- $\DeltaW_{2}$ = $\frac{\frac{e^{2}}{9}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the electric potential at the third vertex due to the other two electrons, $V_{3}$:

- $V_{3}$= 2 ×$\frac{q}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $V_{3}$ = $\frac{\frac{2}{3}e}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ **[1 mark]**

Work done bringing third electron into the triangle, $\DeltaW_{3}$:

- $\DeltaW_{3}$ = *q*($V_{3}-V_{\infty}$)
- $\DeltaW_{3}$ =`1 third e x ( (2 / 3 e)/(4 pi epsilon _ 0 r) - 0 )`
- $\DeltaW_{3}$ =$\frac{\frac{2}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate total work done in forming the electron:

- $\DeltaW$ =  $\DeltaW_{2}+\DeltaW_{3}$
- $\DeltaW$ =  $\frac{\frac{1}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}+\frac{\frac{2}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{\frac{3}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{3e^{2}}{9r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{e^{2}}{3r}$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *To form the electron, we take each of the three charges from infinity and place them in the corners of the triangle.  When the first electron is brought from infinity to its position there is **no work done** as there are **no other charges**. *

> *When the second electron is brought from infinity into its position it has to do work against the repulsive force of the first electron. *

> *When the third electron is brought from infinity into its position it has to do work against the repulsive force of both the first and second electrons.*

Fig. 1.3 shows the structure of an electron gun. Electrons are released from a cathode with zero kinetic energy and are accelerated towards an anode.

The electrons leave the electron gun at 10% of the speed of light. Calculate the potential difference between the cathode and the anode.
parts.solution_md:
From data page:

- Rest mass of electron, $m_{e}$= 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
- Speed of light in free space, *c *= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the kinetic energy of the electrons when they leave the electron gun, $E_{k}$ :

- $E_{k}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$m$( v_{e} )^{2}$
- $E_{k}$ =$\frac{1}{2}$ (9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup>) × (0.1 × 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup>)<sup>2</sup>
- $E_{k}$ = 4.10 × 10<sup>−16 </sup>J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the potential difference between the anode and the cathode, Δ*V*:

- Work done, Δ*W* = *Q*Δ*V*
- Δ*V* = $\frac{\DeltaW}{Q}$

  - The work done is equal to the gain in kinetic energy
- Δ*V* =$\frac{4.10\times10^{-16}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}$
- Δ*V* = 2562.5 = 2 560 V **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

**Extract:**

Two spheres are identical to the sphere in (b) with the same charge. The spheres are held in a vacuum so that their centres are separated by a distance of 0.52 m. Assume that the charge on each sphere is a point charge at the centre of the sphere.

The two spheres are now released simultaneously so that they are free to move.

Describe and explain the subsequent motion of the spheres.
parts.solution_md:
The subsequent motion of the spheres is:

**Final answer:** **Any ****three ****from:**

- The force between them is repulsive, so the spheres move apart; **[1 mark]**
- The force is in the direction of motion, so there is acceleration and the speed increases; **[1 mark]**
- The potential energy is converted into kinetic energy so the speed increases; **[1 mark]**
- The force decreases with distance, so the acceleration decreases; **[1 mark]**
- Momentum is conserved (at zero) (and the masses are equal) so velocities are always equal and opposite; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**
